bib.title: Co-Evolving LLM Decision and Skill Bank Agents for Long-Horizon Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Co-Evolving LLM Decision and Skill Bank Agents for Long-Horizon Tasks" (COS-PLAY), Xiyang Wu, Zongxia Li, Guangyao Shi, Alexander Duffy, Tyler Marques, Matthew Lyle Olson, Tianyi Zhou, Dinesh Manocha. Preprint, arXiv:2604.20987v1, 22 Apr 2026. Note: the PDF says "Preprint", not peer reviewed. Your note's frontmatter does not list 2604.20987.

COVERAGE: 26 of 26 pages, 85,893 of 85,893 chars read (main text, references skimmed, Appendices A-I, Figs 4-10 text). Extraction was clean. Figure images were not viewed; only their text layers.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Co-evolving a decision agent and a skill bank beats frontier LLMs on single-player games. An 8B model has a higher average reward than all four frontier baselines.
  number: avg reward 924.4 vs GPT-5.4 717.4, GPT-OSS-120B 672.6, Claude-4.6-Sonnet 529.3, Gemini-3.1-Pro 489.3. The "25.1%" in the text is not 924.4/717.4 (that is +28.9%). It matches the unweighted mean of the per-game gains over GPT-5.4: 2048 +41%, Tetris +11.5%, Candy +21.8%, Mario +26.2%. This is my arithmetic, not stated in the paper.
  setup: Qwen3-8B, SFT cold start on 60 GPT-5.4 seed trajectories per game, then GRPO. Games: 2048, Tetris, Candy Crush, Super Mario Bros. 16 evaluation rollouts, 95% CIs.
  quote: "COS-PLAY achieves a substantial average improvement of 25.1% over GPT-5.4 on single-player games over 16 runs."
  where: p.8, section 5.1
- The gain comes from co-evolution, not from skills or RL alone. Ablations that pair a policy with a skill bank from a different training stage do worse than the plain base or SFT model.
  number: Avg reward: Qwen3-8B 379.6; SFT w/o skill 409.5; SFT + 1st skill 465.7; SFT + final skill (no co-evolution) 359.5; GRPO w/o skill 359.9; GRPO + 1st skill 305.2; COS-PLAY 924.4.
  setup: same four single-player games. The Avalon and Diplomacy columns show no consistent gain from any variant.
  quote: "Variants with mismatched skill banks perform worse, as the policy and skill bank are optimized for different state distributions, making retrieved skills less aligned and often harmful."
  where: p.9, section 5.2, Table 1
- The skill bank is a managed library with a lifecycle. Five operations act on it: refine, materialize, merge, split, retire. New skills sit in a buffer until evidence accumulates.
  number: in Diplomacy the bank stayed at roughly 55-70 active skills while 121 were discovered overall and 53 redundant skills were removed by merge/split.
  setup: Diplomacy training, Fig. 3c caption.
  quote: "the active bank stays at roughly 55–70 skills, while 121 are discovered overall. Periodic curation removes 53 redundant skills via merge and split, keeping the bank compact and effective."
  where: p.9, Fig. 3
  note: Table 2 gives a different count, "DIPLOMACY64" skills (cross-run). Treat it as the paper's own inconsistency or a different measure.
- A skill is a structured protocol, and its effect contract is verified before it is written back. Contracts keep only consensus effects across instances. A contract is written back only if its pass rate is high enough.
  number: worked example is EXPLORE, 26/28 pass, rate 0.93. A sporadic effect seen in 5/28 episodes was dropped.
  setup: Diplomacy (Austria) walkthrough, Fig. 2d.
  quote: "We keep only consensus effects that appear consistently across instances, treating infrequent ones as noise." and "only contracts with sufficiently high pass rates are written back into the skill bank."
  where: p.6-7, section 4.2; Fig. 2
  protocol fields: Summary, Pre-condition, Plan, Success/Abort Criteria, Contract.
- Learned skills are reused, not memorised. Reuse is concentrated but not total.
  number: Gini 0.498-0.718. Avg instances per skill 12.7-49.2. Avg contract versions per skill 2.0-6.4.
  setup: Table 2, six games.
  quote: "These results suggest that our framework learns reusable and adaptable skill abstractions rather than memorizing isolated trajectories."
  where: p.10, Table 2
  caution: reuse counts do not prove the skills cause the gains.
- The paper's mechanism claim for Diplomacy is that skills work as a temporal schedule that gives a floor, not a ceiling. Compare an observed difference between runs, not an intervention.
  number: min supply centres 3 vs GPT-5.4 min 1; GPT-5.4 collapses to 3 SC or fewer in 16/60 episodes (27%); COS-PLAY stagnates at 3 SC in 5/28. Action repeat rate 22% in successes vs 40% in failures. Action #1 is picked in 85% of steps.
  setup: Diplomacy case study (Austria), COS-PLAY vs GPT-5.4. Appendix I, Figs 9-10.
  quote: "Skills provide a floor, not a ceiling—they prevent collapse (min=3 vs. GPT-5.4 min=1) even with poor action selection"
  where: p.25-26, Figs 9-10
  also: the EXPLORE to SETUP switch fires at step 5 (µ=5.0, σ=0.0, 28/28 episodes). The authors say "The model uses step number, not center count, as its primary switch signal—transitions are time-driven."
- Separate LoRA adapters per function beat merged adapters. This is the one direct test of keeping the roles apart.
  number: Candy Crush reward 648.8 (split) vs 502.5 (merged LoRAs). Merged is below base Qwen3-8B at 519.9.
  setup: Candy Crush only. Decision agent has 2 adapters (retrieval, action); skill-bank agent has 3 (segmentation, contract, curator). All trained with GRPO.
  quote: "When diverse objectives are compressed into a single adapter, the learned capacity must be shared across incompatible functions, which can cause interference."
  where: p.17-18, Table 6
- Adaptation is cheap and general reasoning is mostly preserved.
  number: at most 25 iterations per game. MMLU-Pro 61.99% to 61.15%; Math-500 EM 46.40% to 44.60%.
  quote: "absolute drops of only 0.8% on MMLU-Pro and 1.8% on Math-500"
  where: p.8, p.19, Table 7
- Social games: competitive but not superior.
  number: Avalon win rate 39.0 (±9.4) vs GPT-5.4 65.0, Gemini 42.0, GPT-OSS and Claude 40.0. Diplomacy mean SC 2.96 vs Gemini 2.72, GPT-5.4 4.70.
  setup: opponent GPT-5.4 for evaluation, GPT-5-mini for training. 10 rollouts per player.
  quote: "inducing at least 8.8% better performance over GEMINI-3.1-PRO"
  where: p.8, p.16-17
  caution: the text says Avalon trails "by only 1%". The table gap to Gemini is 3 points.

Reward design (App. F, useful mechanism): the action reward combines the environment reward, a skill-following shaping term with λ_f = 0.1, and a switching cost. The skill-retrieval reward is delayed, computed at skill-switch time, and includes a contract-completion term and an abort penalty. The curator reward includes an exploration term "to prevent systematic rejection of new skills." All reward computations are "CPU-only and require no additional LLM inference."

LIMITS
- Authors concede: reliance on compact text-based state summaries. "Over long trajectories, summarization errors can accumulate, reducing skill relevance." No multimodal tests. Cross-domain transfer is future work.
- Authors concede: exact replication "may vary across API versions", because opponents are black-box APIs.
- Not shown, my reading:
  - Games only. No coding, tool-use or web agents. No held-out games or transfer between games.
  - The skills are trained into weights by GRPO, so this is not a file-rewrite evolve loop.
  - There is no matched-compute or retry baseline. Frontier models get no skill bank, and COS-PLAY gets a GPT-5.4 SFT warm start. So the comparison is not like-for-like.
  - Many CIs overlap. 16 rollouts. Example: Mario COS-PLAY 948.9±153 vs GPT-OSS 968.5±175. Avalon 39.0±9.4 vs GPT-5.4 65.0±14.2.
  - No ablation of the skill-bank agent's maintenance operations (merge, split, retire) individually. No ablation of contract verification.
  - Reuse is evidenced only by descriptive Table 2. No measure of skill activation or adherence, which is the point of your Lin et al. metrics.
  - Mechanism claims (Fig. 10) are post-hoc case studies on one power (Austria).
  - The word "contract" here means a learned state-change specification, not a success definition like your note's evolve-loop Contract.
  - Dated: model names are GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.6-Sonnet.
- Relevance to note 08: it supports "rewrite skills, not weights" only in part. Here the skills are a curated, versioned library while the weights are also trained. The paper's evidence that policy and skill bank must be updated together (stale or mismatched banks hurt) fits the note's "plasticity vs stability" and "activation vs adherence" points.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Voyager (Wang et al., 2023, skill library); Group-in-Group Policy Optimization (Feng et al., 2025) and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024); LoRA (Hu et al., 2022); skill trees (Konidaris et al., 2010); SkillsBench (Li et al., 2026a); SoK: Agentic Skills (Jiang et al., 2026b); Agent Skills survey (Xu & Yan, 2026); SkillRL (Xia et al., 2026); SAGE (Wang et al., 2025a); PolySkill (Yu et al., 2025b); MemRL (Zhang et al., 2026b); MemSkill (Zhang et al., 2026a); CASCADE (Huang et al., 2025b); ProcMEM; XSkill; AgentEvolver (Zhai et al., 2025, for metrics); Orak and lmgame-bench (environments).

CODE: none. The code URL is https://github.com/wuxiyang1996/COS-PLAY. The paper says "We will release" it.

FIGURES (captions read, images not viewed)
- Fig 1 (p.4): COS-PLAY overview. Decision agent, skill bank agent and skill bank, with equations 1-3: s̃_t=π_skill(o_t,B), z_t=π_int(o_t,s̃_t), a_t~π_act(·|o_t,z_t,s̃_t). Shows the loop quickly.
- Fig 2 (p.6): skill pipeline on one Diplomacy episode (boundary proposal, segmentation, contract learning, maintenance, stored entry). Best single view of the mechanism.
- Fig 3 (p.9): skill bank evolution over Diplomacy training (categories, intention mix, bank growth 55-70 active vs 121 discovered).
- Fig 4 (p.20): training reward curves. Single-player rises steadily. Multi-player self-play is flat, which the authors attribute to symmetric improvement.
- Fig 9-10 (p.25-26): failure analysis (stagnation vs collapse) and retrieval stress test with the causal table.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions in the PDF.
- Table text extracted as run-together strings, but values were legible and cross-checked across Table 1 and Tables 4-5.
- Internal inconsistencies noted above: 25.1% versus the table averages; Diplomacy skill count of 64 in Table 2 versus 121 discovered in Fig. 3c; Avalon "1%" versus the table.
- Pages 20-26 hold figure text only.
